paragraphs: Estimating a treatment’s causal effect often requires assumptions that go beyond the observed data. Methods using an instrumental variable commonly impose a particular outcome structure, such as an additive error model, to obtain a single identifiable answer. This paper instead pursues partial identification: finding a range of causal effects compatible with the observations and the assumptions being made.

The authors develop a method for bounding causal effects in continuous distributions, addressing settings where treatment itself can vary continuously. Their approach uses advances in gradient-based optimization to handle objectives that are otherwise computationally intractable. The motivation is also to accommodate varying amounts of knowledge about the shape of the causal effect, allowing stronger background assumptions to support more informative bounds.

On synthetic and real-world data, the reported bounds contain the causal effect in cases where additive methods fail. The contribution is therefore a way to obtain useful, qualified answers without forcing every problem into the same structural model. The output is a range of possibilities rather than an unjustifiably precise single estimate.
neurips-2020-a-class-of-algorithms-for-g.tldr: The paper develops gradient-based methods for bounding causal effects with continuous treatments, avoiding reliance on a single additive outcome model.

paragraphs: Sparse phase retrieval asks how to recover a signal with few nonzero entries when measurements reveal only magnitudes. The missing phase information makes the recovery problem nonconvex. This paper studies a continuous-time version of mirror descent applied to an unconstrained batch objective using squared measurements and a squared-error loss.

The central result is a convergence guarantee for a particular geometry, specified by the hypentropy mirror map. Recovery is proved for a k-sparse signal when its smallest nonzero entry has magnitude on the order of the signal’s Euclidean norm divided by the square root of k. Under that condition, the required number of Gaussian measurements scales as k squared, apart from logarithmic factors.

The approach matters because it adapts to sparsity without adding a regularization penalty or explicitly thresholding entries. The paper also connects the analysis to Hadamard Wirtinger flow: gradient descent using a Hadamard parametrization arises as a first-order discrete-time approximation to mirror descent. This supplies a theoretical explanation for that related method while keeping the recovery claim tied to its stated assumptions.
neurips-2020-a-continuous-time-mirror-de.tldr: Continuous-time mirror descent recovers sparse signals from magnitude-only Gaussian measurements under stated signal conditions, without thresholding or regularization.

paragraphs: Large integer programs can be difficult to solve even with carefully engineered optimization software. This paper asks whether a learned strategy can organize the work of an existing solver more effectively. Its objective is practical: improve elapsed solution time while retaining the benefits of established solver implementations.

The framework uses large neighborhood search. At each iteration, it selects a subset of decision variables for optimization and holds the other variables fixed. An existing solver handles the resulting subproblem. The choice of which variables to revisit becomes a separate decision, and the authors show that a useful selector can be learned from training data.

This division of labor gives machine learning a focused role: choosing where the solver should spend its effort. The solver still supplies its optimization machinery within each chosen neighborhood. In extensive empirical evaluation, the framework significantly outperforms commercial solvers such as Gurobi in wall-clock time. The finding supports learned search organization as an effective way to improve solver performance on the evaluated problems, rather than requiring a new solver built from scratch.
neurips-2020-a-general-large-neighborhoo.tldr: A learned neighborhood selector helps existing integer-programming solvers achieve substantial wall-clock improvements in empirical evaluations.

paragraphs: In a two-player zero-sum game, one player’s gain is the other’s loss. A stable solution may require each player to randomize among actions, because a pure Nash equilibrium needs conditions that often fail in practice. Although mixed equilibria exist more broadly, finding them through mirror descent becomes difficult in high dimensions.

The paper represents each mixed strategy as a collection of weighted particles. Particle positions describe the available choices, while their weights describe how much probability each receives. Both are updated through gradient descent-ascent. The authors study these updates as interacting flows over probability measures using the Wasserstein-Fisher-Rao metric, connecting the finite representation to a broader mathematical description.

The theoretical results include a law of large numbers linking particle behavior to mean-field dynamics. For a related Langevin gradient-ascent dynamic, the paper establishes global convergence to an approximate equilibrium. These are distinct claims about related dynamics. The method also identifies mixed equilibria in high dimensions and demonstrates effectiveness when training mixtures of generative adversarial networks.
neurips-2020-a-mean-field-analysis-of-tw.tldr: Weighted particle strategies make mixed-equilibrium search tractable in high dimensions, with mean-field theory and demonstrated applications to GAN mixtures.

paragraphs: A task-oriented dialogue system needs to understand a user’s request, choose an action, and generate a response. These responsibilities often motivate separate models. SimpleTOD asks whether one language model can perform them together by expressing all of the subtasks as parts of a single sequence prediction problem.

The model is causal: it predicts subsequent sequence content from what has already appeared. This shared formulation allows the system to benefit from pretraining in open-domain language modeling, including models such as GPT-2. The architectural contribution is the unification itself, making the dialogue subtasks compatible with the same training and prediction mechanism.

On MultiWOZ, SimpleTOD improves the previous state of the art in joint goal accuracy for tracking dialogue state. The authors also report robustness to noisy annotations in that setting. In end-to-end evaluation, inform rate increases by 8.1 points, success rate by 9.7 points, and the combined score by 7.2 points. Together, these results show that a simple unified formulation can improve both state tracking and the evaluated action-and-response outcomes.
neurips-2020-a-simple-language-model-for.tldr: SimpleTOD treats dialogue understanding, action selection, and response generation as one language-modeling problem and improves MultiWOZ results.

paragraphs: Target propagation is an alternative to backpropagation motivated partly by questions about how multilayer learning could occur in the brain. Its learning behavior has been less well understood mathematically. This paper analyzes target propagation through optimization theory to clarify what kind of update it performs and where an established variant encounters trouble.

The analysis links target propagation closely to Gauss-Newton optimization, showing that its mathematical character differs substantially from backpropagation. It also identifies a fundamental limitation of difference target propagation when a neural network is non-invertible. This is a relevant setting because the analysis explicitly concerns networks where information cannot simply be recovered by reversing the forward computation.

The authors propose a new reconstruction loss to improve training of feedback weights and offer an initial solution to that limitation. Their formulation also allows direct feedback connections from the output to individual hidden layers. Experiments support the theory, showing significant improvements over difference target propagation in performance and in how closely forward-weight updates align with loss gradients. The reported comparison concerns that variant, rather than establishing superiority over backpropagation.
neurips-2020-a-theoretical-framework-for.tldr: An optimization analysis exposes a limitation of difference target propagation and motivates a reconstruction loss that improves its feedback learning.

paragraphs: A bandit learner repeatedly chooses an arm and receives feedback about that choice. Here, the underlying rewards are fixed by an adversary without knowledge of the learner’s policy. A separate attacker can then alter the reward observed for the selected arm, subject to a limited corruption budget. The paper studies how this extra interference changes achievable learning performance.

The authors first establish a regret lower bound for algorithms that know the attacker’s budget. They also prove an impossibility result for algorithms that lack this information: even a budget growing more slowly than the time horizon can prevent a guarantee of sublinear regret. Thus, a relatively small total amount of corruption does not by itself ensure that a budget-agnostic learner can learn successfully.

Their proposed algorithm, ExpRb, combines a biased reward estimator with a parameter controlling robustness. Its regret is characterized in terms of the corruption budget. When that budget is known, the regret bound is tight, connecting the algorithm’s performance to the theoretical limit established for this setting.
neurips-2020-adversarial-bandits-with-co.tldr: The paper establishes limits for corrupted bandit feedback and introduces ExpRb, whose regret is tight when the corruption budget is known.

paragraphs: Batch normalization allows residual networks to be trained at much greater depths. This paper explains that benefit by examining the relative sizes of a block’s residual branch and skip connection at initialization. The skip connection passes information through, while the residual branch supplies the part that changes it.

The authors show that batch normalization scales down the residual branch relative to the skip connection by a factor on the order of the square root of network depth. Consequently, early in training, normalized residual blocks in deep networks compute functions close to the identity on average. The qualification matters: the result describes their average behavior, rather than requiring every block to act exactly as an identity mapping.

Using this explanation, the authors develop a simple initialization scheme that enables training deep residual networks without normalization. Their empirical study also separates this depth benefit from the ability to use larger learning rates. Larger learning rates help only in particular compute regimes, and their benefit is minimal with small batches. The findings therefore make the value of normalization more specific to initialization and training conditions.
neurips-2020-batch-normalization-biases-.tldr: Batch normalization helps deep residual networks by initially weakening residual branches, an insight that also enables normalization-free initialization.

paragraphs: Some optimization problems evaluate a decision by its risk under uncertain environmental conditions. This paper considers objectives defined by either value at risk or conditional value at risk, calculated from an expensive black-box function. A decision and a random environmental variable jointly determine the function’s outcome, so the quantity being optimized depends on a distribution of possible outcomes.

The proposed algorithms exploit this structure rather than modeling the final risk objective directly. They place a Gaussian-process model on the underlying function of the decision and environment. That model induces uncertainty about the risk measure, and the algorithms use this implied posterior to choose which function evaluations to perform next.

This distinction matters when evaluations are costly: the sampling strategy uses information about the process producing the risk, not just isolated values of the resulting objective. The authors introduce a family of Bayesian optimization algorithms and report substantial improvements in sampling efficiency. Numerical experiments demonstrate their effectiveness across multiple problems. The framework is motivated by decisions under uncertainty, including portfolio optimization and robust systems design.
neurips-2020-bayesian-optimization-of-ri.tldr: Modeling the underlying uncertain function with a Gaussian process improves the sampling efficiency of Bayesian optimization for VaR and CVaR objectives.

paragraphs: Pedestrian detection becomes difficult when people overlap or hide parts of one another. The paper attributes much of this difficulty to representing each person with an axis-aligned rectangle. Such a box gives an approximate location and size, but treats the enclosed region uniformly, making it hard to distinguish overlapping people from the surrounding visual noise.

The authors introduce Beta Representation, which describes a pedestrian using a two-dimensional beta distribution. It explicitly relates the full-body box to the visible box and gives different pixels different probability values. This emphasizes the center of visible mass, providing more information about where the person’s visible evidence lies than a uniform rectangle supplies.

A companion suppression strategy, BetaNMS, uses the representation to better distinguish heavily overlapping instances. The full Beta R-CNN pipeline adds BetaHead and BetaMask components to exploit it. The reported outcome is improved detection in crowded and occluded scenes. The contribution ties the object representation to the process of distinguishing competing detections, addressing the ambiguity that arises when several people occupy much of the same image region.
neurips-2020-beta-r-cnn-looking-into-ped.tldr: Beta R-CNN represents pedestrians with spatial probability distributions to better distinguish overlapping people in crowded and occluded scenes.

paragraphs: This paper studies copying the behavior of an image classifier when access is limited to its output class probabilities. The original training images are unavailable, and gradients cannot be propagated through the classifier. The goal is to train a student model that reproduces the black-box teacher’s functionality with little loss of accuracy.

The method first learns to generate images from a proxy dataset whose images and classes differ from those used to train the teacher. It then applies an evolutionary strategy to generated samples, seeking images that elicit a strong teacher response for a particular class. These samples provide useful material for transferring the teacher’s behavior to the student without needing access to the teacher’s internal computation.

Experiments on three benchmark datasets compare the framework with several existing methods. The authors report better performance than the considered baselines and, generally, better results than state-of-the-art methods that do have internal access to the teacher. These empirical findings show that carefully generated training examples can make probability-only access sufficient for effective distillation in the evaluated settings.
neurips-2020-black-box-ripper-copying-bl.tldr: Generated images refined through evolutionary search enable effective model distillation using only a black-box teacher’s class probabilities.

paragraphs: When sampling sequentially from a finite population without replacement, uncertainty changes as more distinct items are observed. That uncertainty may determine when to stop collecting data. The paper develops confidence sequences: successive confidence sets that become smaller while simultaneously containing the target parameter with high probability across the sampling process.

The simultaneous guarantee is central. It addresses uncertainty throughout data collection, rather than only at one predetermined sample size. The authors give a general construction that uses Bayesian quantities to obtain a frequentist confidence sequence. The key mathematical property is that the ratio of the prior to the posterior, evaluated at the true parameter, forms a martingale.

The paper also develops Hoeffding-type and empirical-Bernstein-type bounds, including both time-uniform confidence sequences and fixed-time intervals. These improve on previous bounds and explicitly measure the advantage of sampling without replacement. Together, the results provide tools for reporting uncertainty as observations accumulate, with guarantees that account for the finite population and the fact that previously sampled items cannot be drawn again.
neurips-2020-confidence-sequences-for-sa.tldr: The paper constructs tighter uncertainty bounds that remain valid throughout sequential sampling without replacement.

paragraphs: A visual dialogue agent needs to adapt its behavior to a new task while continuing to communicate intelligibly with people. Adaptation can create linguistic drift: the agent’s language changes in ways that undermine human understanding. This paper studies learning visually grounded dialogue from visual question-answering data and adapting to new tasks without language-level supervision.

The model separates intention from language. This factorization gives the system a way to change what it is trying to accomplish while limiting disruption to how it expresses itself. The approach addresses a practical data problem: adapting conversational behavior would be less costly if each new task did not require a fresh collection of language-supervised dialogue examples.

The authors evaluate adaptation through qualitative examples, automated measures, and human studies. All three forms of evidence show that the proposed model can adapt to new tasks while retaining language quality. The compared baselines either perform poorly on the new tasks or drift toward language that people cannot understand. The findings support separating communicative intent from expression as a useful design choice in this setting.
neurips-2020-dialog-without-dialog-data-.tldr: Separating intention from language helps visual dialogue agents adapt without language-level supervision while preserving human-readable communication.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning often becomes more manageable when values or policies can be expressed through a small set of features. But assuming those features are already available leaves a major question unanswered: how should an agent learn them? This paper addresses that question under the assumption that the environment’s unknown transition matrix has low rank.

The authors connect learning a representation to a particular nonlinear matrix decomposition problem. They also clarify the relationship between low-rank Markov decision processes and latent-variable models. This structural analysis shows that low-rank models substantially extend earlier representation-learning formulations, including block MDPs, giving the learning problem a broader mathematical foundation.

Their algorithm, FLAMBE, combines exploration with representation learning and provides provably efficient reinforcement learning for low-rank transition models. Its analysis also removes reachability assumptions used in earlier results for the simpler block-MDP setting. The contribution therefore concerns both what kinds of environments can be represented and how an agent can learn within them. The efficiency claim remains tied to the low-rank model assumption.
neurips-2020-flambe-structural-complexit.tldr: FLAMBE jointly explores and learns representations for provably efficient reinforcement learning under a low-rank transition assumption.

paragraphs: Learning heuristics for graph optimization is useful only if they can handle the sizes and constraints of practical problems. This paper focuses on two gaps: scaling to billion-sized graphs and making combinatorial choices under a budget. GCOMB is designed to address both while preserving the quality of the resulting solutions.

The framework combines two learning components. A graph convolutional network is trained through a probabilistic greedy mechanism to estimate node quality. A Q-learning component then addresses the combinatorial decision problem, with importance sampling used to make that component more efficient. This combines assessments of individual nodes with a learning mechanism for the broader selection task.

Experiments on real graphs report that GCOMB is 100 times faster than the compared state-of-the-art methods for learning combinatorial algorithms, with marginally better solution quality. In an influence-maximization case study, it is 150 times faster than the specialized IMM algorithm while achieving similar quality. These findings describe the evaluated comparisons and show a substantial empirical efficiency gain without a corresponding loss of solution quality.
neurips-2020-gcomb-learning-budget-const.tldr: GCOMB combines graph neural prediction and efficient Q-learning to accelerate budget-constrained graph optimization while maintaining solution quality.

paragraphs: Generating a realistic image does not automatically give a model control over the underlying camera or object pose. Earlier approaches using intermediate voxel representations faced a tradeoff: low image resolution or incomplete separation between scene properties and viewpoint. In the latter case, changing the camera could also change the apparent identity of the object.

GRAF introduces a generative model based on radiance fields. This representation avoids confining the scene to a coarse three-dimensional grid and supports separating camera properties from scene properties. The authors also describe graceful degradation when reconstruction is ambiguous. A discriminator operating on patches at multiple scales enables high-resolution synthesis while the model learns from two-dimensional images without supplied camera poses.

The authors evaluate the approach systematically on synthetic and real-world datasets. Their experiments show that the resulting models can generate high-fidelity images with three-dimensional consistency. The contribution connects a representation previously successful for new views of a single scene to generative image modeling, making viewpoint control and consistent scene identity part of the image-synthesis problem.
neurips-2020-graf-generative-radiance-fi.tldr: GRAF learns generative radiance fields from unposed images to synthesize high-resolution views with consistent three-dimensional scene properties.

paragraphs: Cooperating agents can become stuck when they improve their policies one at a time. An individually unhelpful change may become useful if a teammate also changes. With incomplete information, coordinating such updates is especially difficult because an earlier policy change can alter which later situations are reached.

The paper introduces policy-change density to decompose changes in overall game value into policy changes at individual information sets. Joint Policy Search uses this decomposition to improve collaborative policies without reevaluating the entire game. In the tabular settings discussed, it is proved not to worsen performance and can improve solutions produced by unilateral methods. An online form connects the approach to gradient updates when game states cannot be fully enumerated.

For Contract Bridge bidding, JPS improves a strong self-play baseline by strengthening cooperation between teammates. Against WBridge5, it achieves an advantage of 0.63 IMPs per board over 1,000 games, compared with the previous reported state-of-the-art advantage of 0.41. These results provide empirical evidence for coordinated policy improvement in a large imperfect-information game, alongside the tabular guarantees.
neurips-2020-joint-policy-search-for-mul.tldr: Joint Policy Search coordinates collaborative policy updates through a local decomposition of game-value changes and improves competitive bridge bidding.

paragraphs: An agent may need to understand how its present situation arose, as well as predict what happens next. Standard General Value Functions represent predictive knowledge, such as expected fuel use on a future trip. They do not answer the retrospective question of how much fuel a car is expected to have when observed at a particular place and time.

That second question depends on possible histories: when the tank was filled and how the car reached its current location. The paper introduces Reverse General Value Functions to represent knowledge about these past influences on the present. It also introduces Reverse Reinforcement Learning as the procedure used to train those representations.

The distinction changes the direction of the question being learned, from consequences of the current situation to historical factors associated with it. The authors demonstrate empirical utility in representation learning and anomaly detection. These findings indicate that retrospective information can be useful for constructing learned descriptions and identifying unusual behavior. The contribution is a framework for representing that information, rather than merely asking an ordinary predictive value function to answer a different question.
neurips-2020-learning-retrospective-know.tldr: Reverse Reinforcement Learning trains value functions that describe past influences on the present, with demonstrated uses in representation learning and anomaly detection.

paragraphs: This paper studies the theoretical scope of neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent. Its central result states that they can learn in polynomial time any function class that some algorithm can learn in polynomial time. The claim includes parity functions, which are important here because they distinguish the capabilities of different learning frameworks.

The universality result remains valid under the gradient-noise conditions considered by the authors, including possibly polynomial-scale noise. This establishes a separation from statistical query algorithms, which do not have comparable universality in cases such as parities. It also shows that SGD-based deep learning is not constrained by the classic limitations of the perceptron.

A complementary lower bound on generalization error identifies a boundary to this robust universality. When gradients are averaged across sufficiently large batches, as in full gradient descent, the robust universality property breaks down. Thus, the result concerns the computational capabilities of SGD-based learning and the role of its gradient information. It does not assert that every network or arbitrary training configuration will efficiently learn every tractable problem.
neurips-2020-on-the-universality-of-deep.tldr: SGD-trained neural networks are theoretically universal among polynomial-time learners, but the robust result breaks down with sufficiently large gradient batches.

paragraphs: Allocating donor organs involves both predicting patient outcomes and deciding how to use a scarce resource. Each organ is different, and patients can respond differently to the same organ. A policy that chooses the best immediate match may therefore overlook how scarcity affects the total benefit available across the waiting population.

OrganITE combines estimates of potential patient-organ outcomes with an explicit model of organ scarcity. Its assignment decisions account for both, extending beyond greedy policies that optimize life years for the organ currently available. The authors also introduce an individualized treatment-effect model designed to handle the high-dimensional space of organ characteristics, addressing the prediction problem underlying those decisions.

Tests on real and simulated data show increased total population life years compared with the greedy approaches considered. The reported improvement reaches as much as an additional year of life expectancy relative to existing assignment policies. This is a result from the evaluated settings, not a promised benefit for every recipient. The paper’s central contribution is linking individualized outcome estimates to scarcity-aware allocation.
neurips-2020-organite-optimal-transplant.tldr: OrganITE combines patient-specific outcome estimates with organ scarcity to improve population life-year outcomes in real and simulated evaluations.

paragraphs: A three-dimensional point cloud describes geometry through sampled points, while feature edges provide a more structured description of that geometry. PIE-NET is an end-to-end learnable method for identifying these edges robustly. It represents the results as parametric curves, including straight lines, circles, and B-splines, rather than treating edge identification solely as a collection of point-level decisions.

The network uses a region-proposal architecture with two stages. The first produces an over-complete set of candidate edge and corner points. The second ranks the proposals to determine which should be retained. This separates generating a broad set of possibilities from deciding which candidates deserve inclusion in the inferred edge structure.

The authors train and evaluate PIE-NET on the ABC dataset of CAD models. They compare it with traditional processing pipelines and the learning-based edge detector EC-NET. The reported improvements are significant in both quantitative measurements and qualitative inspection. The contribution combines learned proposal selection with a curve-based output representation, producing explicit geometric edge descriptions from point-cloud input.
neurips-2020-pie-net-parametric-inferenc.tldr: PIE-NET learns to recover parametric feature curves from point clouds using candidate proposals and learned ranking.

paragraphs: A regression system normally produces a numerical prediction for every input. This paper allows it to abstain, while fixing the proportion of cases it may reject. The question is then how to spend that rejection allowance so that predictions on the remaining cases are as good as possible.

The authors derive an optimal rule based on thresholding the conditional variance, which describes how variable the outcome is for a given input. They then propose a semi-supervised procedure with two datasets. Labeled examples estimate the regression function and conditional variance; a separate unlabeled dataset calibrates the threshold to achieve the desired rejection rate.

The resulting predictor is shown to approach the optimal reject-option predictor in both risk and rejection rate. The paper also applies the procedure to k-nearest-neighbor regression and establishes convergence rates under mild conditions. A numerical study illustrates its benefit. The contribution therefore links the decision to withhold a prediction to an explicit statistical quantity and provides a way to calibrate how often withholding occurs.
neurips-2020-regression-with-reject-opti.tldr: Regression with a fixed abstention rate can use conditional variance to decide when to reject, with labeled estimation and unlabeled calibration.

paragraphs: Variable selection must balance finding genuinely relevant variables against selecting irrelevant ones. For the Lasso, this paper characterizes that balance through false discovery rate and power. Its goal is a complete diagram separating combinations of these quantities that the method can achieve from combinations it cannot.

The characterization is asymptotic and applies to random-design regression in a regime of linear sparsity. Within that setting, the authors identify all attainable pairs of false discovery rate and power. The tradeoff persists regardless of signal strength, so making the underlying signals stronger does not remove the restrictions described by the diagram.

The paper completes earlier work by identifying two additional simple constraints on the possible pairs. The refinement is especially substantial above the Donoho-Tanner phase transition. Extensive simulations support the sharpness of the resulting boundary. This gives a more precise account of the Lasso’s variable-selection capabilities: it describes the joint limits on discoveries and mistakes, with the theoretical conclusion explicitly tied to the stated asymptotic regression setting.
neurips-2020-the-complete-lasso-tradeoff.tldr: The paper completes the asymptotic Lasso tradeoff between false discoveries and power under random designs and linear sparsity.

paragraphs: Online algorithms make decisions as information arrives, without having the complete problem available in advance. Predictions can offer guidance about the next action, but their usefulness depends on their accuracy. This paper studies how to incorporate such advice while retaining performance guarantees when the guidance is misleading.

The authors extend the primal-dual method, a framework for designing online algorithms, so that predictions can influence its decisions. They use the extension to construct algorithms for a variety of online covering problems. The contribution is therefore a shared design framework rather than a prediction mechanism tailored to just one problem.

The analysis compares algorithmic costs with both the true offline optimum and the predicted offline optimum. These comparisons make the value of accurate advice and the consequences of inaccurate advice part of the same performance account. With accurate predictions, the resulting algorithms outperform what online algorithms can achieve without that advantage, while maintaining good guarantees when predictions mislead. The central result is this combination of improved performance under useful advice and protection under poor advice.
neurips-2020-the-primal-dual-method-for-.tldr: A prediction-aware primal-dual framework improves online covering performance with accurate advice while retaining guarantees when advice is misleading.

paragraphs: Flexible molecules can adopt many geometries, and finding representative collections of these conformations is computationally demanding. The problem matters for understanding relationships between molecular structure and activity. TorsionNet approaches conformer search as a sequence of decisions learned through reinforcement learning, under the rigid rotor approximation.

The model is trained using curriculum learning and aims to maximize the Gibbs Score, a new evaluation quantity grounded in thermodynamics. The paper also investigates the theoretical benefit of the curriculum. This connects the search policy’s learning objective to a thermodynamic measure, giving the sequential procedure a specific target for judging the conformations it discovers.

In the reported experiments, TorsionNet outperforms the highest-scoring chemoinformatics method by a factor of four on large branched alkanes and by several orders of magnitude on lignin. It also surpasses Self-Guided Molecular Dynamics, described as more exhaustive and computationally intensive. These are performance comparisons on the evaluated search tasks, rather than stated runtime speedups. The results support learned sequential search for difficult molecular systems within the method’s approximation.
neurips-2020-torsionnet-a-reinforcement-.tldr: TorsionNet uses curriculum-trained reinforcement learning to search molecular conformations and achieves strong reported results under the rigid rotor approximation.
